files.lesson.md: --- order: 14 unit: lines9 node: AC9M9A03 n2 uses: [AC9M9A03 n1] assumes: [AC9M9A03 n1] connection: car-park-lines title: Parallel and perpendicular summary: "Parallel lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to −1: turn one upside down and change the sign." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Every line in a car park has to be parallel or at a right angle to its neighbour. Can the plan check that with numbers alone?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8361 url: http://127.0.0.1:8361/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- Parallel lines never meet and perpendicular lines cross at a right angle. You can tell which a pair is from their gradients alone. ## Predict: parallel? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing on a pair of lines that look about parallel shows who trusts the picture and who compares the gradients." check: type: predict q: "On a car-park plan, one line goes through (0, 1) and (4, 3). Another goes through (1, 0) and (5, 2). Are the lines parallel?" options: - "Yes: they go up at the same rate" - "No: they start at different places" - "No: one is longer" - "You can't tell without drawing them" actual: "Yes. The first goes up 2 for 4 across, so its gradient is 2 ÷ 4 = ½. The second also goes up 2 for 4 across: ½. Same gradient, so they're parallel." ``` Do the two lines ever meet? Think about how fast each one rises. ## Run: match the gradient ```step stage: run insight: "Sliding the gradient of one line against a dashed line shows that equal gradients never meet, whatever the starting point." try: { playground: board, starter: "pair.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Move $m$ so the solid line is parallel to the dashed line. Was your prediction right?", when: "m = 2" } ``` The dashed line is $y = 2x + 1$. Change $m$ in the solid line, $y = mx$, until the lines never meet. ## Investigate: parallel and perpendicular ```step stage: investigate insight: "Parallel lines share a gradient. A perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal: turn it upside down and change the sign, so the two multiply to −1." tasks: - check: type: question q: "A line goes through $(0, 1)$ and $(2, 7)$. Another goes through $(1, 0)$ and $(3, 6)$. Are they parallel?" options: ["Yes: both have gradient 3", "No: one has gradient 3 and the other 6", "No: they start at different places", "You can't tell"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Check the second: it rises 6 over a run of 2.", "Different starting places don't matter: parallel lines can start anywhere.", "You can tell, from the gradients."] explain: "(7 − 1) ÷ (2 − 0) = 3 and (6 − 0) ÷ (3 − 1) = 3. Same gradient, so parallel." - check: type: number q: "A line has gradient $4$. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?" answer: -0.25 tolerance: 0.001 explain: "Turn 4 (that is 4/1) upside down: 1/4. Change the sign: −1/4, or −0.25. Check: 4 × (−¼) = −1." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. What number times 4 gives −1?", answer: -0.25, tolerance: 0.001, explain: "4 × (−0.25) = −1." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#kai" text: "Kai finds the gradient of a line perpendicular to a line of gradient 3. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: perpendicular-negate-only explain: "Line 2: changing only the sign gives −3, but 3 × (−3) = −9, not −1. Turn it upside down too: −1/3." ``` ### Same gradient Here's finding a perpendicular gradient. ```worked m_1 = \frac{3}{2} :: The gradient of the first line. \frac{2}{3} :: Turn it upside down. m_2 = -\frac{2}{3} :: Change the sign. \frac{3}{2} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -1 :: Check: perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. ``` Now try one on paper: a line has gradient $5$. Find the gradient of a perpendicular line, then type it. ### Upside down and change the sign ### Find the mistake Read Kai's working. What should the second line say? ## Modify: change the lines ```step stage: modify insight: "Moving the solid line to a right angle, then testing the rule at the edges: a flat line." try: { playground: board, starter: "pair.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - hint: ["The dashed line goes up 2 for each 1 across.", "Turn 2 upside down and change the sign."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ so the solid line is perpendicular to the dashed line: the corner is a right angle.", when: "m = -0.5" } - hint: ["Multiply the two gradients.", "Is the answer −1?"] check: { type: question, q: "Two lines have gradients $\\frac{3}{4}$ and $-\\frac{4}{3}$. Are they perpendicular?", options: ["Yes: they multiply to −1", "No: they're both different", "No: only equal gradients are special", "Only if both are positive"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Different gradients can still be perpendicular.", "Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines are the other special case.", "One of the two has to be negative."], explain: "3/4 × (−4/3) = −1, so they're perpendicular." } - hint: ["A flat line has gradient 0.", "What would the perpendicular line look like?"] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: a line is flat, with gradient 0. What is the line perpendicular to it?", options: ["A vertical line, which has no gradient", "A line with gradient 0", "A line with gradient −1", "There isn't one"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "That would be parallel to it.", "That line leans at an angle.", "There is: straight up and down."], explain: "Turning 0 upside down would divide by 0. The perpendicular is vertical, and a vertical line has no gradient." } ``` ### A right angle ### The test ### A flat line ## Practise: parallel or perpendicular? ```step stage: practise insight: "Using gradients to decide, and to build a line with a given relationship." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A line is parallel to $y = 3x + 7$. What is its gradient?" answer: 3 explain: "Parallel lines have the same gradient: 3." - check: type: number q: "A line has gradient $\\frac{1}{2}$. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?" answer: -2 explain: "Turn ½ upside down to get 2, then change the sign: −2." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Turn $\\frac{1}{2}$ upside down. What do you get?", options: ["2", "−½", "½"], answer: 0, explain: "1/2 upside down is 2/1 = 2." } - check: type: question q: "Line A goes through $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 6)$. Line B goes through $(0, 5)$ and $(6, 3)$. Which is true?" options: ["They're perpendicular", "They're parallel", "Neither"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Line A has gradient 3 and line B has gradient −1/3: not equal.", "3 × (−1/3) = −1, so it's more than neither."] explain: "A: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. B: (3 − 5) ÷ (6 − 0) = −1/3. 3 × (−1/3) = −1: perpendicular." - check: type: question q: "Review: what is the gradient of the line through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 8)$?" options: ["3", "1/3", "6", "−3"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That's run over rise.", "6 is the rise; divide by the run, 2.", "The line goes up, so the gradient is positive."] explain: "Rise 6, run 2: 6 ÷ 2 = 3." ``` ### Parallel ### Perpendicular ### Which pair? ### Review From the last lesson: rise over run. ## Make: the car park ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the car park: use gradients to check that the plan's lines are at right angles." tasks: - hint: ["Find each gradient first.", "Then multiply them."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "On a car-park plan, the kerb goes through $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 4)$. A bay line goes through $(0, 6)$ and $(2, 2)$. Work out both gradients, multiply them, and type the product." steps: - ["$\\text{kerb} = \\frac{4 - 2}{5 - 1} = \\frac{1}{2}$", "rise over run for the kerb"] - ["$\\text{bay} = \\frac{2 - 6}{2 - 0} = -2$", "rise over run for the bay line"] - ["$\\frac{1}{2} \\times (-2) = -1$", "the gradients multiply to −1"] answer: "-1" answerLabel: "Product of the gradients" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["1", "The bay line goes down, so its gradient is negative."] - ["-4", "Check the kerb's run: 5 − 1 = 4, so the rise 2 ÷ 4 = 1/2."] criteria: - "I found each gradient as rise over run." - "I took the rise and run in the same order for each line." - "I multiplied them and compared the answer with −1." explain: "½ × (−2) = −1, so the bay line is perpendicular to the kerb." - check: type: question q: "What does the answer tell the builder?" options: ["The bay line meets the kerb at a right angle", "The bay line is parallel to the kerb", "The lines are the same length", "The bay line is too steep"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Parallel lines have equal gradients, not gradients that multiply to −1.", "Gradients say nothing about length.", "Steepness isn't a problem here: only the angle."] explain: "A product of −1 means perpendicular." ``` ### The product Back to the car park. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### What it means The coordinates here are made up for the task. **Also used in** - **Building.** Walls, floors and tiles are laid parallel or at right angles, and a plan can be checked with gradients. - **Computer graphics.** Games need the direction at right angles to a surface to work out how light and bounces behave. - **Next lesson.** The distance between two points: how long is each line? ```teacher summary: Students use gradients to decide whether lines are parallel or perpendicular, and find the gradient of a parallel or perpendicular line (AC9M9A03, node 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can tell parallel lines from their gradients. - I can find the gradient of a perpendicular line by turning it upside down and changing the sign. - I can check a pair of lines against the product of −1. struggle: "Turning the gradient upside down as well as changing the sign. Ask: what do the two gradients multiply to?" before: > Students need Gradient between two points. The one idea: parallel lines have equal gradients, and perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. The common mistake is changing the sign only (Kai's working). The car-park coordinates are made up for the task. The board's axes are about equal in scale, so right angles look right, but trust the numbers over the picture. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 'You can't tell' haven't yet linked gradient to angle." - "Run: ask students to predict m before moving the slider." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the car park in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for both gradients written before the product." - "Modify: before they set m, ask them to say the gradient of the dashed line." stuck: - see: A student answers -3 for a perpendicular to gradient 3. ask: What do 3 and -3 multiply to? fix: "-9. It has to be -1, so turn it upside down: -1/3." - see: A student says two lines are parallel because they look it. ask: What are their gradients? fix: Work them out from the points and compare. stretch: Find the rule of the line through (2, 5) that is perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. support: Fix the gradients as fractions (2/1, 1/2) so that 'upside down' is easy to see. leads: > Continues AC9M9A03 node 2. Where it leads: coordinate geometry proofs in Year 10 (Is this shape a rectangle?). exit: q: A line has gradient 3/5. What is the gradient of a perpendicular line? a: -5/3. explain: > Parallel lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to −1: turn one upside down and change the sign. ```
